decks.title: Computerised Accounting — Part 1: The Computerised Accounting System and How to Use It
goals: Explain the meaning, components and structure of a computerised accounting system and compare it with manual accounting
State the features, advantages and limitations of computerised accounting
Distinguish ready-to-use, customised and tailor-made software and choose one for a business
Design a coding scheme, create groups and ledgers, enter and validate vouchers, and generate the trial balance and final accounts

slides.heading: Computerised Accounting
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **computerised accounting system**: what it is, what it needs, which software to choose, and how a business uses it from **codes** to **final accounts**. Software is described generically.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what a computerised accounting system is, its components and structure, features and limitations, types of software, codes ledgers and vouchers, and reports and security
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: This chapter is the alternative to analysis of financial statements in part B of your paper. In this first part we learn what a computerised accounting system is, what it is made of, its strengths and limits, and the kinds of software a business can choose. Then we follow an imagined shop, Chambal Stationery Mart, from setting up its account codes to printing its final accounts.

slides.heading: Manual and computerised accounting

rows: Journal and subsidiary books written by hand
Voucher keyed in once and saved in a database
Posting to ledger accounts by hand
No posting: ledgers drawn from stored vouchers
Ledgers balanced; trial balance drawn up
Trial balance generated at any moment

visual.alt: Table comparing manual and computerised accounting stage by stage: identifying, recording, classifying, summarising, final accounts and closing
visual.caption: Only recording needs a person to act; the rest is done by the program.

slides.narration: A computerised accounting system keeps the same double entry rules, but the work changes. Each transaction is keyed in once as a voucher and saved in a database. There is no separate posting: ledgers, the trial balance and the final accounts are drawn from the stored vouchers whenever they are asked for. Only recording needs a person; classifying and summarising are done by the program.

slides.heading: Five components

rows: The laid-down steps for collecting, entering, checking and reporting
Bills are entered the same day; reports printed every Saturday
Transactions and master records: ledgers, groups, codes
Nineteen vouchers in April, eighteen ledgers
Users who enter, check and use the records
The owner and one accounts assistant
One desktop, a printer and a backup drive

visual.alt: Table of the five components of a computerised accounting system, procedure, data, people, hardware and software, with an example of each from the imagined Chambal Stationery Mart

slides.narration: Every computerised accounting system has five components. The procedure is the set of steps for collecting, entering and checking records. Data are the transactions and master records such as ledgers and codes. People are the users. Hardware is the computers, printers and storage. Software is the accounting program and its database. Take any one away and the system cannot work.

slides.heading: Structure: input, processing, output

nodes.label: Output: ledgers, trial balance, final accounts, reports

visual.alt: Flow of a transaction through a computerised accounting system: source document, input as a voucher with codes, processing which validates stores and updates, the database, and output as ledgers, trial balance, final accounts and reports
visual.caption: Structure: input → processing → output, around one database.

slides.narration: Follow one transaction. A source document, such as a bill, becomes input when it is keyed in as a voucher with account codes, a date and an amount. Processing checks the voucher, stores it in the database and updates every account it touches. Output is whatever we ask for: a ledger, the trial balance, final accounts or a management report.

slides.heading: Quick check: is there a posting step?
slides.narration: Think back to the comparison table. After a voucher is saved, what still has to be done by hand?

slides.heading: Features and advantages

headers: What it means for the business
rows: Balances and reports are ready the moment vouchers are entered
Totals and balances are computed; unbalanced vouchers are refused
The same rules are applied to every transaction
Ageing of debtors, stock, cash and budget reports from the same records
Years of records kept compactly and searched in seconds
More transactions need little extra staff

visual.alt: Table of features and advantages of computerised accounting: speed and real-time information, accuracy, reliability, management reports, storage and retrieval, scalability and legibility

slides.narration: Why do businesses switch? Reports are ready as soon as vouchers are entered. Totals and balances are computed, so arithmetical slips disappear, and the same rules apply to every transaction. Managers get extra reports, such as which customers owe money for longest. Years of records fit in little space and are found in seconds, and the system grows with the business.

slides.heading: Limitations

rows: Hardware, licences, maintenance and staff training cost money
Fear of change; work slows while two systems run side by side
A crash, power cut or virus can stop all work without backups
A wrong ledger or an omitted voucher still balances
Records can be altered or stolen if access is not controlled
Long hours at screens strain eyes and posture

visual.alt: Table of limitations of computerised accounting: cost of installation and training, staff resistance, system failure, errors of principle and omission not caught, security breaches and health effects

slides.narration: There are limits too. Computers, licences and training cost money. Staff may resist the change, and work slows while old and new systems run together. A crash or a virus can stop everything if there is no backup. And the program cannot judge: a voucher debited to the wrong ledger still balances. Records can be misused if access is not controlled.

slides.heading: Types of accounting software

rows: Standard package bought off the shelf
Standard package modified for the user
Medium firms with some special needs

visual.alt: Table comparing ready-to-use, customised and tailor-made accounting software on meaning, the businesses they suit, cost, training, secrecy and fit

slides.narration: Ready-to-use software is a standard package bought off the shelf. It is cheap, quick to install and easy to learn, and suits small firms. Customised software is a standard package changed to add features a firm needs, which suits medium businesses. Tailor-made software is developed for one organisation alone: costly and slow to build, but an exact fit with high secrecy, so large organisations choose it.

slides.heading: Choosing the software

rows: Can new features, branches or reports be added later?
Price, licences, upgrades and support for the years ahead
How many transactions, users and locations?
How quickly can staff learn it?
Does it produce the statements and analysis management needs?
How tightly must programs and records be protected?
Can records move to spreadsheets or other systems?

visual.alt: Table of factors in choosing accounting software: flexibility, cost of installation and maintenance, size of the organisation, ease of training, utility of reports, expected secrecy and exporting data

slides.narration: Before buying, a business weighs several factors. Is the software flexible enough to grow? What will installation and maintenance cost over the years? How large is the organisation, and how many people will use it? How quickly can staff learn it? Does it give the reports managers need? How much secrecy is expected, and can records be exported to other programs?

slides.heading: Quick check: software for a small grocery
slides.narration: Look at the size of the shop, its needs and its budget, then match them to a software type.

slides.heading: Codification of accounts

rows: One after another as accounts are opened
Each group gets a block of numbers with spare numbers
Letters that recall the account name
SAL salaries, ELE electricity, DRS debtors

visual.alt: Table of three methods of codification: sequential codes, block codes and mnemonic codes, with an example of each
visual.caption: This chapter uses a four-digit block (hierarchical) scheme.

slides.narration: Software works with codes. Codification means giving every account a short, unique code. Sequential codes are simply numbered in the order accounts are opened. Block codes give each group a block of numbers with spare numbers for new accounts. Mnemonic codes are letters that remind us of the name. Good codes speed up entry and let the software group accounts correctly.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a coding scheme for Chambal Stationery Mart
slides.body_md: Chambal Stationery Mart (imagined, Kota) starts business on 1 April 2026. Design a four-digit scheme in which the first digit is the primary head, the second the group and the last two the ledger.

rows: 1101 Furniture and fittings; 1102 Computers and printers
1201 Cash in hand; 1202 Bank account; 1203 Trade receivables

visual.alt: Coding scheme of Chambal Stationery Mart: nine groups from non-current assets at eleven hundred to indirect expenses at fifty-two hundred, with each ledger numbered inside its group
visual.caption: First digit: primary head; second: group; last two: ledger. Gaps leave room for new ledgers.

slides.narration: Here is the scheme. The first digit is the primary head: one for assets, two for liabilities, three for capital, four for income and five for expenses. The second digit is the group, so current assets are twelve hundred and indirect expenses fifty-two hundred. The last two digits number the ledgers, leaving room for up to ninety-nine in each group. Chambal starts with eighteen ledgers.

slides.heading: The hierarchy of account heads

visual.alt: Hierarchy of account heads: the primary head assets, the group current assets, the ledger trade receivables and the individual party accounts under it
visual.caption: Each level sits inside the one above.

slides.narration: The codes build a hierarchy. Assets is a primary head. Inside it sits the group current assets, and inside that the ledger trade receivables. Each customer has a party account under that ledger. When the software prepares a balance sheet, it adds ledgers into groups and groups into heads, so a correct code puts each figure in the right place.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a code
slides.narration: Which first digit did the scheme give to expenses?

slides.heading: Groups, ledgers and voucher types
bullets: Create **groups** under the primary heads, then **ledgers** under groups, each with its code and opening balance.
Enter each transaction through the **voucher type** that fits it.

rows: Money received into cash or bank
Money paid out of cash or bank
Movement between cash and bank only

visual.alt: Table of voucher types in accounting software, receipt, payment, contra, journal, sales and purchase, with what each is used for and an example

slides.narration: Once the company is created, the accountant sets up groups and then ledgers inside them, with codes and opening balances. Transactions are entered through vouchers. Receipts bring money into cash or bank, payments take it out, contra entries move money between cash and bank, and journal vouchers carry non-cash entries and adjustments. Credit sales and purchases have their own vouchers.

slides.heading: Quick check: the right voucher
slides.narration: Which two accounts change when cash is drawn from the bank, and what kind of voucher handles only those two?

slides.heading: Validation: errors stopped at the door

rows: Refused: code 5207 is not in the chart of accounts
Refused: date 2 May 2026 is outside the open accounting period

visual.alt: Table of three vouchers refused by the software: one whose debit and credit amounts differ, one using a code not in the chart of accounts, and one dated outside the open period
visual.caption: Validation stops these errors at the door; the other nineteen vouchers were saved.

slides.narration: When a voucher is saved, the software validates it. Debits must equal credits, every code must exist, the date must fall in the open period, and the voucher type must suit the accounts used. Chambal tried to save twenty-two vouchers; three were refused, one for unequal amounts, one for an unknown code and one dated in May.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: vouchers entered in April
slides.body_md: Chambal enters its April transactions. 19 vouchers pass validation; the first ten are shown. The rest record a cash deposit, rent, electricity, commission, the owner’s drawings, salaries, advertisement and an adjustment for salaries outstanding.

visual.alt: The first ten of the nineteen vouchers of Chambal Stationery Mart for April, from capital paid into the bank to cheques received from customers, each with its codes
visual.caption: Ten of nineteen vouchers shown; codes from the scheme on the previous slide.

slides.narration: Each voucher names its type, date, and the codes and amounts to be debited and credited. Capital and a bank loan come in first, then furniture, computers, purchases and sales. At the month end a journal voucher records rupees ten thousand of salaries still unpaid. Altogether nineteen vouchers are saved, and no ledger is posted by hand.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the trial balance it generates

visual.alt: Trial balance of Chambal Stationery Mart as at thirtieth April generated from nineteen vouchers: eighteen ledger balances with debit and credit totals of 13,88,000 each
visual.caption: Generated, not prepared: the totals agree because every saved voucher balanced.

slides.narration: Now we ask for a trial balance. The software adds every saved voucher into its ledger and lists the balances by code. The totals agree at rupees thirteen lakh eighty-eight thousand, because no unbalanced voucher was allowed in. Cash in hand is rupees ninety-three thousand and the bank balance rupees five lakh twenty-three thousand. Notice that agreement does not prove every voucher went to the right ledger.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 continued: final accounts

visual.alt: Trading and profit and loss account of Chambal Stationery Mart for April in statement form: sales 4,30,000, gross profit 2,04,000 after closing stock of 1,20,000, and net profit 1,31,000
visual.caption: Balance sheet total: ₹10,66,000 on both sides.

slides.narration: With closing stock of rupees one lakh twenty thousand entered, the software prepares the final accounts. Sales of rupees four lakh thirty thousand less purchases and carriage, plus closing stock, give a gross profit of rupees two lakh four thousand. Adding commission and taking away salaries, rent, electricity and advertisement leaves a net profit of rupees one lakh thirty-one thousand. The balance sheet totals rupees ten lakh sixty-six thousand on both sides.

slides.heading: Keeping the records safe

rows: Staff doing more than their job allows
Hidden alteration or deletion of vouchers
Loss of records in a crash or theft
Reading of records if the disk is stolen

visual.alt: Table of security features of accounting software: passwords, user rights, audit trail, backup and restore, locking a closed period and encryption, with what each protects against

slides.narration: Because everything sits in one database, security matters. Each user logs in with a password and is given rights: some may only view, others may enter, and only a few may alter. An audit trail records every change with the user and the time. Regular backups allow recovery after a crash, and a closed period can be locked against changes.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Software + database; record once, report any time
Sequential, block, mnemonic; here 4-digit block codes
Receipt, payment, contra, journal, sales, purchase
Debits = credits, known codes, date in period, right voucher type
Ledgers, trial balance, final accounts generated on demand

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning, components, software types, codification, vouchers, validation and reports of a computerised accounting system

slides.narration: To sum up: a computerised accounting system records each transaction once in a database and produces every report from it. It has five components and runs from input through processing to output. Choose ready-to-use, customised or tailor-made software by size and needs. Code accounts in blocks, enter vouchers of the right type, let validation catch errors, and generate the trial balance and final accounts.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name all **five components**: procedure, data, people, hardware, software.
Compare software types on **cost, size, training, secrecy, fit**.
In a coding scheme, say what **each digit** means and leave **gaps** for new ledgers.
Name the **voucher type** for each transaction: contra for cash ↔ bank only.
A generated trial balance always agrees, but it does **not** prove the right ledgers were used.
slides.narration: Learn the five components by name. When comparing software types, use clear bases such as cost, size of business, training, secrecy and fit. In a coding question, explain what each digit stands for and show gaps for new ledgers. Name the right voucher for each transaction. And remember that a trial balance from the software always agrees, yet it cannot prove every voucher went to the right ledger.

decks.title: Computerised Accounting — Part 2: Electronic Spreadsheets in Accounting
goals: Write spreadsheet formulas with relative references, locked references and names, and use SUM, IF, ROUND and VLOOKUP
Prepare a bank reconciliation statement in a spreadsheet
Prepare depreciation schedules with SLN, written-down value formulas and DDB, and a loan schedule with PMT
Compute accounting ratios with formulas and choose a suitable chart for accounting figures

slides.heading: Electronic spreadsheets in accounting
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **formulas and functions**, and four accounting jobs a spreadsheet does well: **bank reconciliation**, **depreciation**, **loan schedules** and **ratio analysis**, plus **charts**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: cells formulas and references, functions, bank reconciliation, depreciation schedules, loan schedules, and ratios and charts
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: A spreadsheet is a grid of cells in rows and columns. Each cell can hold a label, a number or a formula, and a formula recalculates by itself whenever a figure changes. In this part we learn how formulas and functions work, and then use them for a bank reconciliation, depreciation schedules, a loan repayment schedule, ratio analysis and charts. Every firm is imagined.

slides.heading: Cells, formulas and results

visual.alt: A spreadsheet invoice of the imagined Palar Leather Works: each amount is quantity times rate, the total uses the sum function, a two per cent discount is given by an if test, and the amount payable is 80,948
visual.caption: Each formula cell shows the formula and, after the arrow, what the cell displays.

slides.narration: Here is a small invoice. Columns carry letters and rows carry numbers, so each cell has an address. A formula always begins with an equals sign. Each amount multiplies the quantity by the rate in its own row. The total uses the sum function over a range of cells, and an if test gives a discount only when the total reaches fifty thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Functions used in accounting

rows: Total of the numbers in the range
One of two results, by a test
Labelling a balance favourable or overdraft
Number rounded half away from zero
Rupee interest; ratios to two decimals
Double declining balance charge for a period
Item from the matching row of a table
Finding a ledger from its code

visual.alt: Table of spreadsheet functions used in accounting: sum, if, round, payment, straight-line, double declining balance and vertical lookup, with what each returns and where it is used
visual.caption: FALSE in VLOOKUP asks for an exact match.

slides.narration: Functions are ready-made formulas. The sum function adds a range. The if function chooses between two results by a test. The round function fixes the number of decimals. The payment function gives a loan instalment. The straight-line and double declining balance functions give depreciation. The vertical lookup function finds a row in a table by its first column and returns an item from it.

slides.heading: Relative references, locked references and names

visual.alt: Table showing a relative formula copied down: quantity times rate in D2 becomes the matching formula in D3 and D4, each multiplying its own row
visual.caption: Relative references move with the copy. A rate kept in one cell must be locked (a dollar sign before the column letter and the row number) or given a name.

slides.narration: When a formula is copied, its relative references move with it. That is why one formula for quantity times rate, typed once and copied down, works on every row. But a rate kept in a single cell must not move. Lock it with a dollar sign before the column letter and the row number, or give the cell a name such as Rate.

slides.heading: Quick check: copying a formula
slides.body_md: Choose the formula the copy will produce.
slides.narration: Count how many rows the formula moves, and move each relative reference by the same number of rows.

slides.heading: Looking up a ledger by its code

visual.alt: A lookup on part of the chart of accounts: typing code fifty-two oh one finds the ledger salaries and the group indirect expenses
visual.caption: The code must be in the first column of the table.

slides.narration: The vertical lookup function is handy with a chart of accounts. We give it the code to find, the table to search, the column to return and the word false, which asks for an exact match. Typing the salaries code returns the ledger name in one cell and its group in the next. If the code is missing, the function shows an error.

slides.heading: Quick check: what will the lookup return?
slides.body_md: Read the table and the column number.
slides.narration: Find the row with the code, then count across to the column the formula asks for.

slides.heading: Why the cash book and pass book differ

headers: Starting from the cash book balance
rows: Cheques deposited but not yet credited
Interest credited, direct deposits, dividends collected
Bank charges, interest on overdraft, standing-instruction payments

visual.alt: Table of the causes of difference between the cash book and the pass book and whether each is added or deducted when starting from the cash book balance
visual.caption: With an overdraft, every item moves the other way.

slides.narration: The cash book and the bank pass book rarely agree on the same day. Some items are in the cash book only, such as cheques issued but not yet presented, or deposited but not yet credited. Others are in the pass book only, such as bank charges, interest and direct deposits. A bank reconciliation statement starts from one balance and adjusts for each of these items.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: bank reconciliation in a spreadsheet
slides.body_md: Pennar Electricals (imagined, Nellore): cash book balance ₹1,57,000 on 31 March 2026. Unpresented cheques ₹45,000; deposits not credited ₹32,000; bank charges ₹1,200; interest credited ₹2,400; direct deposit ₹15,000; insurance paid by the bank ₹6,800.

visual.alt: Bank reconciliation of Pennar Electricals in a spreadsheet: cash book balance 1,57,000, add 62,400, deduct 40,000, giving a pass book balance of 1,79,400, labelled favourable by an if test
visual.caption: The same figure is reached by adding up the pass book on its own.

slides.narration: Pennar's cash book shows rupees one lakh fifty-seven thousand. Three items make the bank's figure larger: unpresented cheques, interest and a direct deposit, which total rupees sixty-two thousand four hundred. Three make it smaller: uncredited deposits, charges and an insurance premium, totalling rupees forty thousand. The sheet adds the first sum and deducts the second, giving rupees one lakh seventy-nine thousand four hundred, and an if test labels it favourable.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: depreciation schedules
slides.body_md: Tapti Printers (imagined, Surat) buys a printing machine for ₹5,00,000, with a salvage value of ₹50,000 after 5 years. Compare the straight-line method with the written-down value method at 30% a year, rounding each charge to the rupee.

visual.alt: Depreciation schedules of a printing machine of Tapti Printers costing 5,00,000: straight line gives 90,000 a year down to the salvage value of 50,000; written-down value at thirty per cent falls to 84,035
visual.caption: Cells B1 to B4 are named Cost, Salvage, Life and Rate.

slides.narration: The straight-line function gives rupees ninety thousand every year, so the value falls evenly to the salvage value of rupees fifty thousand. The written-down column multiplies each opening value by the rate, rounded to the rupee, so the charge falls each year, from rupees one lakh fifty thousand to rupees thirty-six thousand fifteen. Each row's opening value is the previous closing value.

slides.heading: Three methods on one chart

visual.alt: Line chart of the book value of the Tapti machine over five years: the straight line falls evenly to fifty thousand, the written-down value falls steeply at first and ends near eighty-four thousand, and the double declining balance falls fastest and stops at the salvage value of fifty thousand
visual.caption: Double declining balance charges: 2,00,000, 1,20,000, 72,000, 43,200, 14,800; the last is cut to stop at salvage.

slides.narration: The chart shows the book value under three methods. The straight line falls evenly. The written-down value falls steeply at first and never quite reaches the salvage value. The double declining balance function uses twice the straight-line rate, forty per cent here, but in the last year it charges only rupees fourteen thousand eight hundred, so the value stops exactly at salvage.

slides.heading: Quick check: rounding interest
slides.body_md: Work out what the cell will show.
slides.narration: Multiply, divide by twelve, then remember how the round function treats an exact half.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a loan repayment schedule
slides.body_md: Kosi Cold Storage (imagined, Purnia) borrows ₹3,00,000 at 12% a year, repayable in 5 equal monthly instalments. Instalments and interest are rounded to the rupee.

visual.alt: Loan repayment schedule of Kosi Cold Storage: a loan of 3,00,000 at twelve per cent a year repaid in five monthly instalments of 61,812; interest falls from 3,000 to 612 and the balance reaches zero
visual.caption: Instalment in B4: `=ROUND(PMT(B2/12,B3,-B1),0)` = 61,812; B1, B2 and B4 are named Loan, Rate and EMI.

slides.narration: The payment function, with one per cent a month for five months, gives an instalment of rupees sixty-one thousand eight hundred twelve. In each row, interest is one per cent of the opening balance, rounded to the rupee, and the rest of the instalment repays the loan. Interest falls from rupees three thousand to rupees six hundred twelve, and after the fifth instalment the balance is exactly zero.

slides.heading: Ratio analysis with formulas

visual.alt: Ratio formulas of Palar Leather Works: current ratio 2, quick ratio 1.25, gross profit ratio 25 per cent and debt-equity 0.3, with an if test comment
visual.caption: Figures in B1 to B7: current assets 9,60,000, inventories 3,60,000, current liabilities 4,80,000, revenue 48,00,000, gross profit 12,00,000, debt 6,00,000, shareholders' funds 20,00,000.

slides.narration: Ratios are natural spreadsheet work. Enter the figures once, then each ratio is a division of cell references, wrapped in the round function to two decimals. For Palar Leather Works the current ratio is two to one and the quick ratio one point two five to one. An if test can add a comment, such as within limit for the debt-equity ratio of zero point three to one.

slides.heading: Choosing a chart

rows: Comparing amounts across items or years
Share of each expense in total cost
Parts of a whole across periods
Cost split for each of four years

visual.alt: Table for choosing a chart: column or bar to compare, line for trends, pie for parts of a whole, stacked column for parts across periods, and scatter for the relation between two measures

slides.narration: Charts turn figures into pictures. Use a column or bar chart to compare amounts across branches or years, a line chart to show a trend over time, and a pie chart to show how one whole is divided into parts. A stacked column shows parts of a whole across several periods, and a scatter chart shows how two measures move together.

slides.heading: A column chart of profit

visual.alt: Column chart of the net profit of Palar Leather Works for four years rising from three hundred thousand to six hundred thirty thousand rupees
visual.caption: Net profit = revenue − expenses: 2023: 32,00,000 − 29,00,000; 2024: 38,00,000 − 33,80,000; 2025: 43,00,000 − 37,80,000; 2026: 48,00,000 − 41,70,000.

slides.narration: Here a column chart compares the net profit of Palar Leather Works over four years. The spreadsheet subtracts expenses from revenue for each year, and the chart is drawn from those cells, so it changes if a figure changes. Profit rises from rupees three lakh to rupees six lakh thirty thousand, which a column chart makes easy to see.

slides.heading: Quick check: which chart?
slides.body_md: Choose the chart that fits the purpose.
slides.narration: Is the manager comparing years, showing a trend, or splitting one total into shares?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: `=B3+B8-B13` with totals by `SUM` and a label by `IF`
`=ROUND(PMT(rate/12,months,-loan),0)`; interest on opening; principal = instalment − interest
Column to compare, line for trends, pie for shares

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: formula patterns for bank reconciliation, depreciation, loan schedules and ratio analysis, and the choice of charts

slides.narration: To sum up: formulas begin with an equals sign and recalculate by themselves. Relative references move when copied; a fixed cell needs a lock or a name. Use sum and if for a bank reconciliation, the straight-line function or a rounded rate for depreciation, the payment function for loan instalments, and rounded divisions for ratios. Pick a chart by purpose: compare, trend or share.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write formulas with **cell references**, starting with **=**, and show what each cell displays.
Lock or name a **rate cell** before copying a formula down.
In a loan schedule, check **interest + principal = instalment** in every row.
In a depreciation table, link each **opening value** to the previous **closing value**.
State the **rounding** you use: ROUND(…, 0) for rupees, ROUND(…, 2) for ratios.
slides.narration: Write every formula with cell references and show the value it produces. Lock or name a rate cell before you copy a formula. In a loan schedule, check that interest plus principal equals the instalment in each row and that the balance ends at zero. In a depreciation table, link each opening value to the last closing value. Always say how you rounded.

notes.title: Computerised Accounting — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The computerised accounting system: meaning, components and structure
sections.body_md:
A **computerised accounting system** records transactions through accounting software into a **database** and produces ledgers, the trial balance, final accounts and other reports from the stored records whenever they are needed. The double-entry rules do not change; the tools and the order of work do.

**Components (five):** procedure, data, people, hardware, software.

**Structure:** *input* (source documents keyed in as vouchers with codes) → *processing* (validation, storage, updating of accounts) → *output* (ledgers, trial balance, final accounts, management reports), all around one database.

**Manual versus computerised:** identification of transactions is the same; recording becomes voucher entry; there is no separate posting or balancing; the trial balance and final accounts are generated; closing is year-end processing.

key_terms.definition_md: A system that records transactions through software into a database and generates accounting reports from it.
An organised store of records that the software reads and updates.
The laid-down steps for collecting, entering, checking and reporting transactions.

nodes.label: Output: ledgers, trial balance, final accounts, reports

visual.alt: Flow of a transaction through a computerised accounting system: source document, input as a voucher with codes, processing which validates stores and updates, the database, and output as ledgers, trial balance, final accounts and reports
visual.caption: Structure: input → processing → output, around one database.

sections.heading: 4. Spreadsheets: cells, formulas, references and functions
sections.body_md:
A **spreadsheet** is a grid of **cells** named by column letter and row number (B4). A cell holds a label, a number or a **formula**, which begins with **=** and recalculates whenever a figure it uses changes.

**References:** a **relative** reference (B4) moves when the formula is copied; an **absolute** reference is locked with a dollar sign before the column letter and before the row number, and does not move; a **name** given to a cell (Rate) also always points to that cell. Use a lock or a name for a single rate or constant.

**Functions used:** `SUM`, `IF`, `ROUND` (half away from zero), `PMT` (instalment; negative for a positive loan, so enter the loan as a negative figure), `SLN`, `DDB` (twice the straight-line rate on the opening value, never below salvage), `VLOOKUP` (with FALSE for an exact match on the first column).

sections.heading: 5. Spreadsheet applications: bank reconciliation, depreciation, loans and ratios
sections.body_md:
**Bank reconciliation statement.** Start from one balance; add the items that make the other book higher and deduct those that make it lower; with an overdraft every item moves the other way. In a sheet, totals are `SUM` ranges and the result is one formula such as `=B3+B8-B13`; an `IF` can label the balance.

**Depreciation (asset accounting).** Straight line: `=SLN(cost, salvage, life)`, equal every year, ending at salvage. Written-down value: charge = `ROUND(opening value × rate, 0)`, opening value = previous closing value. `DDB` charges twice the straight-line rate on the opening value and stops at salvage.

**Loan repayment schedule.** Instalment = `ROUND(PMT(yearly rate ÷ 12, months, −loan), 0)`; each row: interest = `ROUND(opening × rate per period, 0)`, principal = instalment − interest, closing = opening − principal. Check interest + principal = instalment in every row and a closing balance of zero (or a rupee or two of rounding, adjusted in the last instalment).

**Ratio analysis.** Each ratio is a rounded division of cells, for example `=ROUND(B1/B3,2)`; `IF` adds a comment against a benchmark.

sections.heading: 7. Using a computerised accounting system: codes, ledgers, vouchers and reports
sections.body_md:
**Steps:** create the company (name, financial year, password) → create groups and ledgers with codes and opening balances → enter vouchers → enter adjustments (closing stock, outstanding and prepaid items) → generate ledgers, trial balance and final accounts → year-end processing.

**Codification** gives each account a unique code. Methods: **sequential**, **block** (a block of numbers per group, with gaps for new accounts) and **mnemonic** (letters). **Hierarchy:** primary head → group → ledger → party accounts. In this chapter: four digits, first = head (1 assets, 2 liabilities, 3 capital, 4 income, 5 expenses), second = group, last two = ledger.

**Vouchers:** receipt, payment, contra (cash ↔ bank only), journal (non-cash and adjustments), sales, purchase.

**Validation** refuses a voucher whose debits and credits differ, that uses an unknown code, that is dated outside the open period, or whose type does not suit its accounts. A generated trial balance always agrees, but it does not prove the right ledgers were used.

**Security:** passwords, user rights, audit trail, backup and restore, locking of closed periods, encryption.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing a formula without **=**, or with typed figures instead of **cell references**.
- Copying a formula that uses a single rate cell without locking or naming that cell.
- Using PMT with the **yearly** rate for **monthly** instalments (divide the rate by 12).
- Charging written-down depreciation on the **cost** every year instead of the opening book value.
- Adding instead of deducting in a bank reconciliation that starts from an **overdraft**.
- Calling a cash-to-bank deposit a receipt or payment voucher (it is **contra**).
- Claiming that a trial balance that agrees proves the accounts are correct.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a function, a voucher type, a software type, one feature or limitation.
- 3 marks: three features or limitations explained, or a small statement or formula set (1 mark each).
- 4 marks: a comparison on four bases, or a three-year schedule with formulas.
- 6 marks: a full bank reconciliation, depreciation or loan schedule with formulas, a coding scheme, or a trial balance with final accounts; formulas and values carry separate marks.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined bakery chain, Godavari Bakes, asks what makes an accounting system "computerised". The best description is a system in which

options.text_md: the accountant keeps the journal by hand and types only the final accounts on a computer
transactions are entered once through software into a database, and ledgers and statements are produced from it on demand
all vouchers are photographed and stored, but the books are still written by hand
an auditor checks the books once a year with the help of a calculator

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** transactions are entered once through software into a database, and ledgers and statements are produced from it on demand. What makes the system computerised is that recording, classifying and summarising all happen in software working on stored records. Using a computer only to type the final statements does not count.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined trading firm, Pranhita Agencies, Ms Savita Kulkarni enters the day’s vouchers and reads the reports the system produces. Among the components of a computerised accounting system, she belongs to
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** people. The five components are procedure, data, people, hardware and software. Users such as accountants and data-entry staff are the people component. The procedure is the set of steps they follow.

questions.stem_md: Suvarnamukhi Kirana, an imagined neighbourhood grocery, records about thirty transactions a day, needs only standard ledgers, a trial balance and final accounts, and has a small budget and one part-time accountant. The most suitable accounting software for it is

customised software with special modules added
no software at all, since computerised accounting suits only companies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ready-to-use software. A small business with standard needs gains most from a package that costs little, can be installed at once and is easy to learn. Its lower secrecy and limited flexibility matter little at this size.

questions.stem_md: An imagined national railway catering corporation runs thousands of outlets with its own pricing, stock-transfer and reporting rules, and wants its accounting programs and records kept under close control. Which type of accounting software fits it best?

options.text_md: Ready-to-use software bought off the shelf
Customised software adapted from a package
Tailor-made software, developed specially for the corporation
An electronic spreadsheet shared by all outlets

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Tailor-made software, developed specially for the corporation. A very large organisation with unique processes and high secrecy needs justifies software built for it alone. questions.stem_md: Before switching to computerised accounting, the partners of an imagined firm, Tawa Valley Traders, list possible drawbacks. Which item on their list is a genuine limitation of a computerised accounting system?

questions.stem_md: Mr Harish Bhandari, who runs an imagined hardware wholesale business in Haldwani, still keeps his books by hand. Explain any three features of a computerised accounting system that would help his business.
questions.solution_md: Name a feature and link it to the wholesaler’s needs in each point.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Speed and real-time information:** each voucher is processed as it is entered, so balances, the trial balance and statements are available the same day instead of weeks later.
2. **Accuracy and consistency:** the software applies the same rules every time, adds and balances accounts itself and refuses vouchers that do not balance, so arithmetical slips disappear.
3. **Reports for decisions:** from one set of stored records it can produce debtors’ ageing, stock and cash-flow reports, helping him decide whom to chase for payment and what to reorder.
4. *(Also accepted)* Storage of years of records in little space with quick search; easy expansion as transactions grow; legible records; security through passwords and backups.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of an imagined cooperative dairy in Anand is worried that moving to computerised accounting may create new problems. State and explain three limitations she could point out.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct limitations, each with a line on why it matters.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Cost of installation and upkeep:** computers, licences, backup devices and annual maintenance are expensive for a small cooperative, and staff must be trained.
2. **Resistance and disruption:** experienced staff may fear the change or their jobs; work slows down while the old books and the new system run side by side.
3. **Dependence on the system and on security:** a power or hardware failure, a virus or a lost password can stop work, and records can be altered or stolen if access is not controlled.
4. *(Also accepted)* The program cannot judge unusual transactions or errors of principle; long hours at screens can affect health.

Also state (d) one factor, besides cost, that each should weigh before buying.
questions.solution_md: Match the scale and the special needs of each organisation to the software type, then name a further factor in choosing.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Mohana Medicals: ready-to-use software.** It has few transactions and standard needs; a low-cost package that is quick to install and easy to learn is enough, and the low secrecy of a widely sold package does not matter much.

**(b) Tunga Spices Ltd: customised software.** Its needs are mostly standard, but export invoices and foreign-currency accounts require extra features, so a standard package modified for it gives a good fit at moderate cost.

**(c) The electricity board: tailor-made software.** Its tariff and subsidy rules are unique, its volume is very large and its records need tight control; software developed for it alone is costly but is the only full fit.

questions.stem_md: The finance committee of an imagined college trust in Dharwad is planning to computerise its accounts. Explain (a) the meaning of a computerised accounting system, (b) its five components and (c) how a transaction travels through the system from input to output.
questions.solution_md: Define the system, list and explain all five components, then trace one transaction through input, processing and output.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Meaning.** A computerised accounting system records business transactions through accounting software into a database and, by processing those stored records, produces ledgers, a trial balance, final accounts and other reports whenever required. It follows the same double-entry rules as manual accounting; only the tools change.

**(b) Components.**
1. **Procedure** — the laid-down sequence of steps for collecting, entering, checking and reporting transactions.
2. **Data** — the transactions and master records (ledgers, groups, codes) that the system stores.
3. **People** — the users, such as data-entry staff, accountants, managers and auditors.
4. **Hardware** — computers, servers, printers, storage and network devices.
5. **Software** — the accounting programs and the database that stores the records.

**(c) Flow.** *Input:* a source document (receipt, bill, cheque counterfoil) is entered as a voucher with codes, date and amount. *Processing:* the software validates the voucher (debits equal credits, codes exist, date within the period), stores it and updates every affected account. *Output:* on request, it prints ledgers, the trial balance, the trading and profit and loss account, the balance sheet and management reports.

Name the input cells Cost (B1), Salvage (B2), Life (B3) and WRate (B4), put years 1 to 4 in rows 7 to 10, and total the charges in row 11. (a) Write the formulas for each column and show the values. **(a)**

|   | A | B | C | D | E |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 | Year | Straight-line charge | Straight-line closing | Written-down charge | Written-down closing |
| 7 | 1 | `=SLN(Cost,Salvage,Life)` → **36,000** | `=Cost-B7` → **1,24,000** | `=ROUND(Cost*WRate,0)` → **64,000** | `=Cost-D7` → **96,000** |
| 8 | 2 | `=SLN(Cost,Salvage,Life)` → **36,000** | `=C7-B8` → **88,000** | `=ROUND(E7*WRate,0)` → **38,400** | `=E7-D8` → **57,600** |
| 9 | 3 | `=SLN(Cost,Salvage,Life)` → **36,000** | `=C8-B9` → **52,000** | `=ROUND(E8*WRate,0)` → **23,040** | `=E8-D9` → **34,560** |
| 10 | 4 | `=SLN(Cost,Salvage,Life)` → **36,000** | `=C9-B10` → **16,000** | `=ROUND(E9*WRate,0)` → **13,824** | `=E9-D10` → **20,736** |
| 11 | Total | `=SUM(B7:B10)` → **1,44,000** |   | `=SUM(D7:D10)` → **1,39,264** |   |

**(b)** The straight-line method charges the same 36,000 every year and ends exactly at the salvage value of 16,000. The written-down value method charges 64,000 in year 1, falling to 13,824 in year 4; its total of 1,39,264 is 4,736 less than the straight-line total of 1,44,000, so the book value left (20,736) is above the expected salvage value. Computers lose value fastest when new, so the heavier early charges of the written-down method match their pattern of use better.

questions.stem_md: The manager of an imagined resort, Kodaikanal Hill Stay, wants one chart showing what share of last year’s total expenses went on staff, food, power, repairs and marketing. Which chart suits this purpose best?

options.text_md: A column chart of the five expenses over five years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A pie chart. A pie chart shows how one whole is divided into parts, so each expense appears as a slice of total expenses for the year.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A line chart is the best way to show the share of each department in the total sales of an imagined department store for a single year.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A line chart shows a trend over time. Shares of one total in one year are shown by a pie chart, or by a single stacked or 100% bar.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of an imagined handloom cooperative, Kaveri Handlooms, has to present three things to its board: (a) monthly sales for the last two years, to show seasonal ups and downs; (b) this year’s revenue, expenses and profit of its four branches side by side; (c) how this year’s total cost is split among yarn, wages, dyeing, power and transport. Suggest a suitable chart for each and give a reason.
questions.solution_md: Trend over time calls for a line chart, comparison across categories for columns or bars, and parts of one whole for a pie.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Line chart.** Monthly sales over two years form a time series, and a line joining the months shows the rise and fall of the seasons clearly; the two years can be drawn as two lines.

**(b) Clustered column (bar) chart.** Placing the three measures of each branch side by side makes comparison between branches easy, with a different colour for revenue, expenses and profit.

**(c) Pie chart.** The total cost is one whole divided into five parts, and the slices show each item’s share of the total.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Column or bar chart with reason

questions.stem_md: An imagined bookshop uses the four-digit coding scheme of this chapter: the first digit is the primary head (5 for expenses), the second the group (52 for indirect expenses) and the last two the ledger. Rent is 5202, electricity 5203 and advertisement 5204, and 5205 is free. Which code should be given to a new ledger, "Telephone and internet charges"?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 5205. Telephone charges are an indirect (office) expense, so they belong to group 52, and the next free ledger number in that block is 05. A code ending in 00 stands for the group itself, not a ledger.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined crockery shop, Pennaiyar Crockery, enters four vouchers in April 2026 (accounting period 1 to 30 April):

| Voucher | Type | Date | Debit | Credit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-14 | Receipt | 10 April | Cash in hand 26,500 | Sales 26,500 |
| P-07 | Purchase | 12 April | Purchases 45,000 | Trade payables 54,000 |
| P-08 | Payment | 15 April | Rent 18,000 | Bank account 18,000 |
| C-03 | Contra | 18 April | Bank account 20,000 | Cash in hand 20,000 |

Which voucher will the software refuse to save?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** P-07. P-07 fails validation because its debits 45,000 ≠ credits 54,000 (the digits were transposed). The other three balance, use valid codes, fall within the period and follow their voucher-type rules.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined electricals shop, Sutlej Electricals, works in a CAS whose chart of accounts has cash in hand (1201), bank account (1202), furniture (1101), trade payables (2201), sales (4101), purchases (5101) and rent (5202); the open period is 1 to 30 April 2026. The software refuses all three of these vouchers. Give the reason in each case and how it should be corrected.

| Voucher | Type | Date | Debit | Credit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| J-02 | Journal | 5 April | 5209: 4,000 | 1201 Cash in hand: 4,000 |
| P-11 | Payment | 2 May | 5202 Rent: 15,000 | 1202 Bank account: 15,000 |
| C-05 | Contra | 20 April | 1101 Furniture: 12,000 | 1201 Cash in hand: 12,000 |
questions.solution_md: Check each voucher against the validation rules: known codes, date inside the open period, and the voucher type matching the accounts used.

answer.model_answer_md:
- **J-02:** code 5209 is not in the chart of accounts. Create the ledger first (for example a new indirect-expense ledger in the 52 block) or use the right existing code; a cash payment should also go through a payment voucher.
- **P-11:** date 2 May 2026 is outside the open accounting period. Enter it in the May period (or, if the rent was paid in April, correct the date).
- **C-05:** a contra voucher may use only cash and bank accounts; buying furniture for cash is a payment, so it must be entered through a payment voucher debiting furniture and crediting cash.

marking_scheme.step: P-11: date outside the period and correction
C-05: wrong voucher type and correction

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A trial balance generated by a computerised accounting system proves that every transaction has been recorded in the correct account.

**Reason (R):** The system accepts only those vouchers in which total debits equal total credits.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** R is true, so the trial balance totals always agree; but A is false, because a voucher debited to the wrong ledger, or a transaction left out altogether, still balances.

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of codification of accounts and describe any two methods of coding, with an example of each for an imagined restaurant, Sabari Kitchen.
questions.solution_md: Define the term with its purpose, then explain two methods, each with an example from a restaurant.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Codification** is giving each account head a short, unique code, built so that its position in the hierarchy (primary head, group, ledger) can be read from it. Codes make data entry faster, avoid confusion between similar names and let the software sort and group accounts.

- **Block (or hierarchical numeric) codes:** each group gets a block of numbers, with spare numbers left for new ledgers; for Sabari Kitchen, 5200–5299 for indirect expenses, so rent is 5202 and gas charges could be 5207.
- **Sequential codes:** numbers given one after another in the order accounts are opened, such as 101, 102, 103; simple but they show nothing about the group.
- *(Also accepted)* **Mnemonic codes:** letters that recall the name, such as KIT for kitchen supplies or SAL for salaries.

questions.stem_md: An imagined school in Siliguri keeps its fee and salary accounts in accounting software that several clerks use. Describe three security features the software should offer.
questions.solution_md: Each feature should say what it protects against.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Passwords and user rights:** each clerk logs in with a personal password, and the administrator decides who may only view reports, who may enter vouchers and who may alter or delete them.
2. **Audit trail:** the software keeps a log of every voucher created, altered or deleted, with the user and the time, so changes can be traced.
3. **Backup and restore:** records are copied at regular intervals to a safe place so they can be restored after a crash, theft or virus attack.
4. *(Also accepted)* Locking of a closed period so that old vouchers cannot be changed; encryption of stored records.

questions.stem_md: Ms Lata Rawat is starting an imagined handicrafts shop in Almora and will keep her accounts in ready-to-use accounting software. Describe, in order, four main steps she will follow from setting up the software to obtaining her final accounts.
questions.solution_md: Set-up, master records, transactions and adjustments, then reports, in that order.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Create the company:** enter the business name, address, the financial year and the date from which books begin, and set a password.
2. **Set up the chart of accounts:** create groups under the primary heads and ledgers under each group (cash, bank, purchases, sales, rent, debtors, creditors and so on), giving each a code and entering opening balances.
3. **Enter vouchers:** record each transaction through the right voucher type (receipt, payment, contra, journal, sales, purchase); the software validates and saves each one, and adjustment entries such as closing stock or outstanding expenses are entered as journal vouchers at the period end.
4. **Generate reports:** display or print the ledgers, the trial balance, the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet; then close the year so that balances are carried forward.

marking_scheme.step: Voucher entry with validation and adjustments
